Chapter 3: Competing Stories—How Culture’s Rituals Shape What People Love
Every day, we’re surrounded by stories about what really matters—but here’s the thing: most of these stories aren’t spoken out loud. They’re woven right into the routines and rituals of our daily lives. Without even noticing, we’re shaped by these cultural “liturgies”—those everyday practices that quietly teach us what to love, what to chase after, and even what to be afraid of.
Picture this—a young professional walks into a high-end store. Soft lighting, just the right music, eye-catching displays. There’s this subtle sense of possibility in the air, right? Like, maybe, just maybe, buying something new is the key to happiness, confidence, or finally fitting in. The whole experience is crafted to stir up desire. It’s more than just the products on the shelves—it’s the message underneath: “You are what you own. Fulfillment is just one purchase away.”
Or think about a sports fan in a packed stadium. The crowd moves together—chanting, cheering, celebrating every victory. There’s this electric sense of unity, of being part of something bigger. The ritual of the game almost feels like worship, shaping what the heart longs for—excitement, triumph, a deep sense of community.
Now, these aren’t just harmless distractions. They’re powerful habits that form us from the inside out. The world is absolutely full of these “secular liturgies”—everyday practices that subtly compete with spiritual formation, each one offering its own version of the good life. They promise meaning, identity, satisfaction… but how often do they leave us feeling restless or empty?
Most of the time, we hardly notice how these rituals are shaping us. We just move through our days, following routines that seem normal—sometimes even necessary. But over time, these little habits carve deep grooves in our hearts, training us to chase after things that never truly satisfy.
And it’s not just the obvious rituals that matter. The way we use technology, how we balance work and rest, even the patterns in how we entertain ourselves—each one sends a message about what’s worth loving. If someone spends hours every day scrolling through news feeds or chasing the next shiny thing, they’re being formed—whether they realize it or not.
Here’s the challenge: these cultural liturgies are everywhere. They’re easy to slip into and tough to resist. Quick rewards, instant gratification, the comfort of fitting in—that’s what they offer. But at the same time, they shape our desires in ways that can pull us away from what’s really good.
So, what do we do? The first step is simply recognizing these competing stories. It’s about paying attention to the habits that are shaping our hearts, and asking some honest questions. Are these routines helping us love what truly matters, or are they training us to chase after lesser things?
This isn’t about rejecting culture or running away from the world. It’s about becoming wise—learning to see how our desires are being shaped, and choosing practices that point our hearts in a better direction. It’s a slow journey, and sometimes it’s pretty tough. But in the end, that’s how we become the kind of people who love what’s truly worth loving.
